question: What is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?
title: Single Responsibility Principle Explained
direct_answer: SRP states that a class should have only one reason to change — meaning it should encapsulate exactly one responsibility. If a class handles user logic, email sending, AND database persistence, any of those three concerns can force a change, making the class fragile and hard to maintain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why separation of concerns matters at the class level and can articulate the 'one reason to change' concept.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defining SRP vaguely as 'do one thing' without explaining what 'one reason to change' means in concrete terms.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete before/after example showing how splitting a class reduces coupling and makes the codebase easier to maintain.

sections.title: What SRP Really Means
sections.content: The **Single Responsibility Principle** is the first of the five SOLID principles and arguably the most foundational. Robert C. Martin defined it as: *a class should have only one reason to change*. This means each class should encapsulate **exactly one responsibility** — one cohesive set of behaviors that serve a single purpose. Think of it like a restaurant kitchen: the chef cooks, the dishwasher cleans, the server delivers food. If one person tried to do all three, any change in any role would disrupt the entire workflow. Similarly, when a Java class handles multiple concerns — say, business logic, data persistence, and email notifications — a change in email configuration or database schema forces you to modify a class that also contains critical business rules. This creates **fragile coupling** and makes maintenance risky. SRP reduces this risk by ensuring each class has a narrow, well-defined purpose.

sections.title: SRP Violation vs. SRP Compliant Design
Key Points
content: **One reason to change**: A class following SRP has exactly one axis of change — if email logic changes, only EmailService changes, not UserService.
**Cohesion**: SRP increases cohesion by grouping related behaviors together and excluding unrelated ones from the same class.
**Coupling**: Violating SRP creates hidden coupling — a database schema change shouldn't require touching email-sending code, but it does when they live in the same class.
**Testability**: SRP makes unit tests simpler because you mock fewer dependencies — testing UserService doesn't require database or email infrastructure.
**Maintenance**: When each class has one responsibility, you know exactly where to look when a requirement changes — email issues go to EmailService, validation issues to UserService.
**Not about method count**: SRP doesn't mean one method per class; a UserRepository can have save, findById, delete, update — all serve the single responsibility of data access.
**Real-world smell**: Classes with names like UserManagerAndEmailSender or imports from javax.mail and java.sql in the same file are SRP violations.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The Single Responsibility Principle says a class should have only one reason to change. That means each class encapsulates exactly one responsibility or concern. Let me give you a concrete example. Imagine you've got a UserManager class that validates user input, saves data to a database, and sends a welcome email. That's three different responsibilities. Now, if your email provider changes from SendGrid to AWS SES, you have to modify UserManager — even though it also contains critical business logic and database code. That's risky. You could accidentally break validation while fixing email config. With SRP, you'd split this into three classes: UserService for business rules, UserRepository for database access, and EmailService for emails. Now each class has one reason to change. If email logic changes, only EmailService changes. This makes the code safer to modify, easier to test, and simpler to understand. A common mistake freshers make is thinking SRP means one method per class. That's not it. A UserRepository can have save, findById, delete, and update methods — that's still one responsibility, which is data access for users. The key question to ask is: why would this class change? If you get multiple independent answers like database schema, email templates, and validation rules, you've got an SRP violation.

question: How do you identify an SRP violation in existing code?
title: Identifying SRP Violations in Java Code
direct_answer: SRP violations are visible when a class has multiple unrelated reasons to change — large file size, names containing 'And', or imports from unrelated packages like javax.mail AND java.sql. The real test: ask 'why would this class change?' — more than one independent answer means SRP violation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to spot design smells in real codebases beyond just theoretical knowledge.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only giving theoretical signs without practical detection strategies like counting imports or analyzing method signatures.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention class size, number of imports, instance variables, or the 'why would this change' test as concrete signals.

sections.title: Practical Detection Strategies
sections.content: Identifying **SRP violations** in real code requires a mix of mechanical checks and conceptual analysis. In production Java codebases, SRP violations don't announce themselves with compiler errors — they show up as **maintenance pain** and **testing difficulty**. The most reliable technique is the **'why would this class change?' test**: list all the reasons a class might need modification. If you can name more than one independent reason — like 'database schema changes' AND 'email template updates' — you've found a violation. But there are also **code smells** that signal trouble before you even analyze logic: unusually large files (500+ lines), class names with conjunctions like 'ManagerAndSender', and import statements spanning unrelated domains. For example, a class importing both `javax.mail.*` and `java.sql.*` is almost certainly doing too much. Spring Boot apps often violate SRP in controller methods that handle HTTP parsing, business logic, and data formatting in one endpoint.

sections.title: Identifying SRP Violations in Real Code
Key Points
content: **'Why would this change?' test**: List all independent reasons a class might need modification — more than one reason means SRP violation.
**Class size**: Files over 300-500 lines often indicate multiple responsibilities crammed together, though size alone isn't proof.
**Import diversity**: A class importing from javax.mail, java.sql, and com.payment.api is juggling three unrelated concerns.
**Instance variable count**: More than 5-7 instance variables often means the class is managing multiple contexts (database, email, cache, etc.).
**Name conjunctions**: Class names with 'And', 'Manager', 'Handler', 'Helper', or 'Util' are code smells suggesting multiple responsibilities.
**Method cohesion**: If methods in a class don't share instance variables, they probably belong in separate classes — low cohesion signals SRP violation.
**Testing pain**: If writing a unit test requires mocking a database AND an email service AND a payment gateway, the class violates SRP.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The most reliable way to spot an SRP violation is to ask: why would this class change? If you can list multiple independent reasons, you've found a problem. For example, if a class changes when the database schema updates, when email templates change, and when payment APIs get upgraded, that's three reasons to change — a clear SRP violation. But there are also mechanical signals you can look for. Check the import statements. If you see javax.mail and java.sql in the same class, that's a red flag. The class is handling both email and database concerns. Look at the class name. Names with conjunctions like OrderProcessorAndEmailSender or ManagerAndValidator usually indicate multiple responsibilities. Check the file size. A 600-line class is almost always doing too much. Count the instance variables. If a class has a DataSource field, an EmailSession field, and a PaymentClient field, it's managing three different external systems — that's too many concerns. In Spring Boot apps, I often see SRP violations in controller methods that parse HTTP requests, run business logic, and format JSON responses all in one method. The testing pain is another giveaway. If your unit test setup needs to mock a database, an email service, and a payment gateway just to test one method, the class definitely violates SRP.

question: How does SRP improve testability of Java classes?
title: SRP and Unit Testability in Java
direct_answer: SRP improves testability because a class with one responsibility has fewer dependencies to mock and a narrower test surface. When a class does three things, a unit test must set up mocks for all three concerns even when testing only one — SRP eliminates that overhead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Connection between design principles and practical testing outcomes — whether you see design as enabling testing, not just code organization.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying SRP is only about code organization without linking it to concrete testing benefits like reduced mock setup.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete example comparing setup for a 3-dependency class vs three 1-dependency classes, highlighting mock count difference.

sections.title: The Testing Connection
sections.content: **SRP directly impacts testability** because each dependency a class has represents setup overhead in your unit tests. When a class follows SRP, it has a **narrow surface area** — it collaborates with only the dependencies needed for its single responsibility. This means your test setup is minimal: mock one or two collaborators, verify the behavior, done. But when a class violates SRP by handling multiple concerns, it accumulates dependencies from all those concerns. A class that validates input, saves to a database, sends emails, and logs to a monitoring service needs **four mocked dependencies** in every test — even if you're only testing the validation logic. This creates **test brittleness**: a change in email logic forces you to update tests for validation logic, even though they're unrelated. SRP eliminates this coupling. When you split responsibilities into separate classes, each test focuses on one thing, mocks only what's necessary, and remains stable when unrelated code changes.

sections.title: Testing Impact: SRP Violation vs. Compliant
Key Points
content: **Fewer mocks**: A class with one responsibility typically needs 0-2 mocked dependencies; a class with three responsibilities needs 5+ mocks in every test.
**Test focus**: SRP lets you test one concern in isolation — validation tests don't need database mocks, repository tests don't need email mocks.
**Setup simplicity**: When each class has one responsibility, test setup is straightforward — you mock only what the responsibility needs to collaborate with.
**Test stability**: Changes to email logic don't break validation tests when they live in separate classes following SRP.
**Faster tests**: Classes with fewer dependencies run faster tests because there's less mocking infrastructure and fewer interactions to stub.
**Clearer failures**: When a test fails in an SRP-compliant class, you immediately know which responsibility broke — no detective work across multiple concerns.
**Pure functions**: SRP often produces classes with no external dependencies at all, like validators or calculators, which need zero mocks and run instantly.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: SRP makes testing way easier because it reduces the number of dependencies you need to mock. Let me show you why that matters. Imagine you have a class that validates orders, saves them to a database, and sends confirmation emails. That's three responsibilities. Now you want to write a unit test for just the validation logic. Even though you're only testing validation, you still have to set up mocks for the database repository and the email service. You have to stub their behavior with when-then-return statements, even though they're completely irrelevant to the validation test. That's wasted effort. Worse, if the email service interface changes, your validation tests break even though validation logic didn't change. That's brittle. When you follow SRP, you'd have three separate classes: OrderValidator, OrderRepository, and EmailService. Now your validation test only needs the OrderValidator class. No mocks at all if it's pure logic. It runs instantly and never breaks unless validation rules actually change. Your repository test mocks just the database, and your email test mocks just the email infrastructure. Each test focuses on one thing and mocks only what that thing depends on. This makes tests faster to write, faster to run, and more stable over time. That's the practical benefit of SRP — it's not just theory, it directly improves your testing experience.

question: What is the difference between SRP and separation of concerns?
title: SRP vs Separation of Concerns in Java
direct_answer: Separation of Concerns is the broad architectural principle that different concerns should be handled by different parts of the system — it applies at every level. SRP is SoC applied specifically at the class level, stating each class should encapsulate exactly one concern. SRP is a concrete application of SoC.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of understanding — can you distinguish related principles and explain how they relate hierarchically?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating SRP and SoC as identical or using them interchangeably without recognizing the scope difference.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give examples at different levels: layered architecture or package structure for SoC, class design for SRP, showing the hierarchy.

sections.title: Scope and Relationship
sections.content: **Separation of Concerns (SoC)** is a fundamental architectural principle stating that a system should be divided into distinct sections, each addressing a separate concern. It's a **universal design guideline** applicable at every level: architecture, modules, packages, classes, and even functions. **SRP**, on the other hand, is SoC **applied specifically at the class level** — it's the SOLID principle that operationalizes SoC for object-oriented design. Think of SoC as the philosophy and SRP as one concrete implementation of that philosophy. For example, a **layered architecture** with presentation, business, and data layers is SoC at the architectural level. Within that architecture, ensuring your `UserService` handles business logic and your `UserRepository` handles data access is SRP at the class level. Both principles fight the same enemy — **tangled responsibilities** — but they operate at different granularities.

rows: All levels: architecture, modules, packages, classes
Class level only — each class one responsibility
Part of SOLID principles (Robert C. Martin 2000)
Class design, method grouping, dependency injection
Does this component handle one concern?
Does this class have one reason to change?
Separate presentation layer from business logic layer

sections.title: When and How to Apply Each
sections.content: Use **SoC thinking** when designing system architecture, module boundaries, or package structure. For example, in a Spring Boot app, you'd separate controller, service, and repository packages — that's SoC at the package level. You'd also separate authentication concerns into a security module and business logic into a domain module — that's SoC at the module level. Use **SRP thinking** when designing individual classes. Ask: does this class have multiple reasons to change? If your `OrderController` is parsing JSON, validating business rules, and formatting responses, that's an SRP violation. Split it into `OrderController` (HTTP handling), `OrderValidator` (business rules), and `OrderResponseBuilder` (formatting). SoC guides the big picture; SRP guides the implementation details. A well-designed system applies SoC at the architectural level and SRP at the class level. They're not competing — they're complementary.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Hierarchical relationship**: SoC is the overarching principle; SRP is SoC operationalized at the class level within object-oriented design.
**Different granularity**: SoC applies to architecture, modules, packages, and classes; SRP applies specifically to classes and their methods.
**Same goal**: Both aim to reduce coupling and increase cohesion by preventing different concerns from tangling together.
**Architectural SoC**: Layered architecture (presentation, business, data) and microservices (order service, payment service) are SoC at system level.
**Class-level SRP**: Splitting UserManager into UserService, UserRepository, and EmailService is SRP at class level.
**Verification test**: SoC asks 'does this component handle one concern?'; SRP asks 'does this class have one reason to change?'
**Not synonyms**: Saying 'SRP is just SoC for classes' is correct, but using them interchangeably ignores the important scope distinction.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Separation of Concerns and SRP are related but not the same thing. Separation of Concerns is a broad architectural principle that says different concerns should be handled by different parts of the system. It applies at every level. For example, in a web app, you separate the user interface from business logic from data access. That's SoC at the architectural level. You also separate authentication logic into a security module and payment logic into a billing module. That's SoC at the module level. SRP, on the other hand, is SoC applied specifically at the class level. It's one of the SOLID principles and it says each class should have exactly one reason to change. So if you have a UserService class, it should only handle business logic for users, not also send emails or access the database. That's SRP. Think of it this way: SoC is the philosophy, and SRP is one concrete way to apply that philosophy when designing classes. A well-designed Spring Boot app uses SoC to organize packages into controller, service, and repository layers. Then within each layer, it uses SRP to ensure each class handles only one responsibility. For instance, OrderService handles business rules, OrderRepository handles database access, and OrderValidator handles input validation. All three are SoC at the package level, and each class following SRP at the implementation level.

question: Can a class have multiple methods and still follow SRP?
title: Multiple Methods and SRP Compliance in Java
direct_answer: Yes — a class can have many methods and still follow SRP as long as all those methods serve the same single responsibility. A UserRepository with save, findById, delete, and update has four methods but one responsibility: data access for User. Method count is irrelevant; concern count is what matters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you truly understand SRP vs naive 'one method per class' misinterpretation that would make code impractical.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking SRP means a class should have only one method, which would lead to absurdly granular classes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish clearly between method count and responsibility count, giving examples of cohesive multi-method classes.

sections.title: Methods vs. Responsibility
sections.content: A common misconception among Java freshers is that SRP means **one method per class** — as if having multiple methods automatically violates the principle. This is completely wrong and would lead to unworkable code with hundreds of tiny classes. **SRP is about responsibilities, not method count.** A class can have five, ten, or even twenty methods and still perfectly follow SRP, as long as all those methods contribute to the **same single responsibility**. The key question is: do all these methods work together to fulfill one cohesive purpose? A `UserRepository` is the classic example: it has `save()`, `findById()`, `findAll()`, `delete()`, `update()`, `existsByEmail()` — that's six methods. But they all serve **one responsibility**: data access for the User entity. None of those methods handle email sending, validation, or business logic. They're all cohesive. The responsibility is 'manage User persistence', and every method supports that responsibility. That's textbook SRP. The test isn't 'how many methods?' but 'how many independent concerns?'

sections.title: Multi-Method Class Following SRP
Key Points
content: **Responsibility, not method count**: SRP cares about how many concerns a class handles, not how many methods it has — a 20-method class can follow SRP.
**Cohesion test**: If all methods use the same instance variables and serve the same purpose, they're cohesive and belong together in one class.
**Repository pattern**: A typical Spring Data repository has save, findById, findAll, delete, update, existsBy methods — all serve one responsibility: data access.
**Service methods**: A DiscountCalculationService might have calculateSeasonalDiscount, calculateLoyaltyDiscount, applyPromotionCode — all serve pricing logic.
**Shared state**: If methods in a class share instance variables, they likely belong together — they're operating on the same responsibility's state.
**One reason to change**: Ask why the class would change — UserRepository changes only when User persistence needs change, not when email or validation logic changes.
**Anti-pattern**: Creating UserSaver, UserFinder, UserDeleter, UserUpdater as separate classes is absurd over-fragmentation, not good SRP.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Absolutely, a class can have many methods and still follow SRP. The principle is about responsibilities, not method count. Let me give you a concrete example. A UserRepository in a Spring Boot app typically has save, findById, findAll, delete, update, and maybe existsByEmail. That's six methods. But it's still following SRP because all those methods serve one single responsibility, which is data access for the User entity. They're all cohesive. None of those methods send emails or validate business rules or format JSON. They all deal with persistence. That's one concern. The key test is to ask: why would this class change? UserRepository changes when the database schema changes or when we switch from JDBC to JPA. That's one reason to change. It doesn't change when email templates update or when validation rules change. So it follows SRP. The mistake freshers make is thinking SRP means one method per class. That would be absurd. You'd end up with UserSaver, UserFinder, UserDeleter as separate classes, which is ridiculous over-fragmentation. Instead, think about whether all the methods in a class work together toward the same goal. If they do, they're cohesive and they belong in the same class. A DiscountService might have calculateLoyaltyDiscount, calculateSeasonalDiscount, and applyPromotionCode. That's three methods but one responsibility: pricing logic. That's perfectly fine SRP.
